claims.claim: Gerlach argues that the reader of The Book of the Long Sun comes to occupy its city as its inhabitants do, rather than being given an explanatory overview of it.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: we begin to inhabit much as the characters do
claims.routeHint: gwern.net raw PDF fetched with a browser user agent; text extracted locally with the macOS Quartz PDF text layer

claims.claim: Gerlach observes that the clues to the nature of Wolfe's world are so sparse that the reader's attention moves off the world question and onto the plot.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: clues are so sparse the reader will focus elsewhere
claims.routeHint: gwern.net raw PDF fetched with a browser user agent; text extracted locally with the macOS Quartz PDF text layer

claims.claim: Gerlach describes the fictional world of the Long Sun as built out of dense particulars, including street names that recur.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: dense and intricate, rich in detail

claims.claim: Gerlach notes that Wolfe estranges his setting by giving ordinary English words unfamiliar in-world applications rather than by coining new ones.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: familiar with are applied in unusual, usually comical ways
claims.routeHint: gwern.net raw PDF fetched with a browser user agent; text extracted locally with the macOS Quartz PDF text layer

claims.claim: Gerlach shows that the in-text dramatis personae preface bound into each volume of The Book of the Long Sun revises its own entry for the god called the Outsider from volume to volume, so that the record corrects itself without any narrator announcing the correction.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: subsequent volumes offer a truer picture
claims.routeHint: gwern.net raw PDF fetched with a browser user agent; text extracted locally with the macOS Quartz PDF text layer

claims.claim: Gerlach says Wolfe's text pushes the reader to form hypotheses about the identity of the Outsider on minimal evidence.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: develop hypotheses about who the Outsider is from minimal clues

claims.claim: Gerlach observes that Wolfe's viewpoint character accepts as ordinary the event the reader is questioning, so the gap between what the character believes and what the reader infers is carried by the character's incuriosity rather than by narratorial comment.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: does not question whether the Chenille he knows could be possessed

claims.claim: Wolfe says that very few readers grasp that the narrator of Peace is dead, a fact the novel signals only through its opening sentence about a fallen elm.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Melissa Mia Hall, Amazing Science Fiction Stories, September 1981; reprinted as chapter 3 of Peter Wright (ed.), Shadows of the New Sun: Wolfe on Writing/Writers on Wolfe, Liverpool University Press, 2007
claims.quote: This is something very few people seem to understand about Peace
